slides.title: A score needs an operating envelope
body: Week 09 / H1 / 2 November 2026
Explain error before trusting a prediction.
slides.teach: Open with the calibration rig: evaluation inside one region does not establish performance outside it. The image is conceptual AI artwork, not measured evidence. Ask students to name a new load, sensor or population that could invalidate a score.

slides.title: Today: explain 60, practise 120
body: H1: 45 min explanation + 15 min hand calculation.
slides.teach: State prerequisites: regression, splitting and MAE from earlier weeks. By the end students must diagnose slices, run fixed-model stress tests and replay a CSV. No new weekly graded homework. H1 analytic tasks are revisited briefly in the notebook, not additional assignments.

slides.title: Which model would you deploy?
body: Model A has lower average error.
Is that enough if rare cases are costly?
slides.teach: Illustrative absolute errors, not notebook measurements. Assume common response units and the same population. A is not automatically preferable: the deployment loss and tolerable tail error matter. Ask for missing group sizes and error costs; do not imply B is universally best.

slides.title: Reliability is conditional evidence
body: Specify population, task and metric.
A reliability claim needs boundaries.
slides.teach: Trace a prediction claim from population to decision. Reliability here means evidence about behavior under stated conditions, not a single universal numerical property. A safety assurance would need a stronger domain-specific process.

slides.title: The evaluated population matters
body: Test risk averages over the test population.
Deployment risk averages over deployment.
slides.teach: Define f as the fixed predictor and L as a specified loss. Finite test MAE estimates a population expectation under sampling assumptions; it is not the population expectation itself. Distribution changes can change the integral even with the same f.

slides.title: Mixtures can hide a weak subgroup
body: Overall MAE is a count-weighted average.
Always retain subgroup sizes.
slides.teach: Derive by partitioning the sum of absolute errors over disjoint exhaustive groups. The identity holds exactly for empirical MAE. It does not hold by averaging subgroup RMSE directly. Group definitions must not silently overlap.

slides.title: Move the mixture, not the errors
body: Keep group MAEs at 1 and 10.
Drag the rare-group fraction.
slides.teach: Ask for the value at 10%, then 25%, before revealing through the slider. Expected answers 1.9 and 3.25. This changes the composition only; no refitting or improvement occurs. This is an analytic example, not an observed model score.

slides.title: Counts constrain interpretation
body: Two errors are not two hundred errors.
Report empty groups as unavailable.
slides.teach: These are illustrative summaries. Same mean does not imply equal uncertainty. With zero rows the mean is undefined, not zero. With two rows report evidence cautiously; a normal-looking point estimate cannot justify a broad population claim.

slides.title: Residual sign changes the story
body: This week: residual = prediction - observation.
Positive means overprediction.
slides.teach: Have students point to the overprediction row. Many texts use observation minus prediction; neither convention is inherently wrong. All plots and code must agree. Absolute-error metrics are unchanged by sign reversal, interpretation is not.

slides.title: MAE preserves response units
body: MAE averages absolute residuals.
It treats each unit of error linearly.
slides.teach: Derive from the residual definition. The metric weights rows equally unless weights are explicitly introduced. Absolute error is appropriate only if its linear penalty matches the evaluation question; do not claim universal superiority.

slides.title: RMSE emphasizes large residuals
body: Square, average, then take a square root.
Keep the order of operations.
payload: RMSE >= MAE on the same rows
slides.teach: Use Jensen or Cauchy-Schwarz intuition for the inequality. RMSE is in response units; MSE is in squared units. One must not square the mean residual or take the mean of signed square roots.

slides.title: One large residual changes the metric
body: Predict the response as the fifth error grows.
Compare MAE with RMSE interactively.
slides.teach: The first four residuals are 0.1,-0.1,0.2,-0.2. A fifth residual t is appended, not substituted. At t=3, n=5, MAE=.72 and RMSE=sqrt(1.82). Even at t=0 the denominator is five; flag this common confusion.

slides.title: A pattern can reveal misspecification
body: True term: x1 squared. Linear approximation: 1.
Residual shape: 1 - x1 squared.
slides.teach: This is a noise-free analytic slice with the other true term canceled, not the actual fitted model. Negative tails indicate underprediction. The curved residual provides a mechanism to look for; observational residuals alone do not prove a physical cause.

slides.title: Covariate shift changes the inputs
body: P(X) changes while P(Y given X) stays fixed.
Error can change even without refitting.
slides.teach: Define covariate shift with the conditional mechanism fixed. The notebook adds the same Gaussian noise law and uses paired base observations. A good model may remain accurate; distribution shift does not necessarily force a specific error increase.

slides.title: Concept shift changes the target rule
body: P(Y given X) changes, even if X does not.
Input-only monitoring can miss it.
slides.teach: This is the synthetic intervention in Task8. It is not a causal discovery. Input histograms remain identical by construction. Actual error assessment needs new outcomes or another justified evaluation procedure.

slides.title: A wider domain exposes a missing term
body: Toy predictor: zero; target: x squared.
For X ~ N(0, sigma squared), MAE = sigma squared.
slides.teach: The expectation follows because absolute residual equals X squared. This population identity is different from the finite uniform-grid exercise and different from the fitted Ridge comparison. Move sigma from1 to3: population MAE1 to9.

slides.title: A range flag is not an error label
body: Observed min/max describe a finite sample.
Gaussian support remains unbounded.
slides.teach: Show a Gaussian shape, observed-range markers and tails. Values beyond the observed training range warrant investigation but are not proof of impossible or incorrect data. A range flag cannot directly measure prediction error.

slides.title: Do not average subgroup RMSEs
body: Pool sums of squares, then take the root.
MAE and RMSE aggregate differently.
slides.teach: Derive by grouping squared errors. With equal groups of RMSE1 and3, pooled RMSEsqrt5, not2. Assumes same response scale and disjoint exhaustive groups. This provides a useful hand-calculation counterexample.

slides.title: Use labels to confirm performance drift
body: Input checks can raise an alert.
Outcome errors answer a different question.
slides.teach: Distinguish operational monitoring signal from measured task performance. Outcomes can arrive with delay or selectively; mention that missing labels can bias conclusions. Do not retrain automatically on an unverified alert.

slides.title: A metric is not a decision rule
body: Choose loss before looking at winners.
Restrict a model when evidence is insufficient.
slides.teach: These are possible actions, not universal engineering safety rules. Ask students what decision costs and tolerance would make an action justified. Fixing a data interface and changing the model are distinct interventions.

slides.title: Intervals need an assumption label
body: Our bootstrap fixes the fitted model.
It resamples IID residuals within a slice.
slides.teach: This descriptive interval conditions on the chosen model and sampling assumptions. It omits training variability and arbitrary future shift. Fewer than two residuals produce no interval in the notebook. Narrowness is not proof of deployment safety.

slides.title: Separate diagnosis from selection
body: Test slices reveal failure patterns.
They must not silently tune the winner.
slides.teach: Protect final evaluation from repeated test-driven adaptation. Predeclared comparisons can be reported without changing the validation-selected winner. Exploratory test patterns motivate a fresh protocol, not a newly unbiased final claim.

slides.title: Task 1: compute before coding
body: 90 errors of 1; 10 errors of 10.
Write total absolute error and overall MAE.
slides.teach: Hand calculation, about two minutes. Expected total190 and MAE1.9. Do not reveal until pairs explain denominators. Stop when each pair has the weighted-sum equation and separate subgroup MAEs.

slides.title: Task 1: change the composition
body: Now use 75 ordinary and 25 rare cases.
Which component changed: model or population?
slides.teach: Peer check for two minutes. Ask why an unchanged model could have a worse dashboard metric. Expected population mixture; do not claim this proves no other change in a real system. Record Task1 prediction/explanation later in the exercise notebook.

slides.title: Task 3: scale a fixed grid
body: Predict the MAE ratio for [-1,1] vs [-3,3].
Use the same 101 normalized grid locations.
slides.teach: Each location is multiplied by3, target magnitude by9. For the zero predictor the absolute residual equals x squared. Hand derive the ratio before using the notebook. Distinguish finite-grid mean.34 from continuous uniform expectation1/3.

slides.title: Task 3: the exact finite-grid check
body: At L=1, grid MAE = 0.34.
At L=3, grid MAE = 3.06.
payload: MAE(L) = L^2 * mean(x_j at L=1 squared)
slides.teach: About two minutes. Endpoints included explain why .34 differs from1/3. The formula uses101points with j0 through100. Stop when students explain why exact9 follows from shared normalized grid, not a universal robustness law.

slides.title: Task 4: calculate the outlier effect
body: Append a fifth error of 3.
slides.teach: Students must choose the correct n. Initial MAE.15,RMSEsqrt(.025). After appending: MAE.72,RMSEsqrt(1.82). Have a partner verify intermediate sums before using a calculator.

slides.title: Task 4: choose a defensible statement
body: RMSE increases more than MAE here.
That does not make either metric universally better.
slides.teach: Two-minute comparison. Ask which loss aligns with high penalty for rare large errors. A chosen metric must fit a stated task, costs and units. Rounded values are display only; calculations use full precision.

slides.title: Summary: qualify every average
body: Report metric, population and group counts.
Use residual patterns to choose the next test.
slides.teach: Use two-minute retrieval: one student explains mixture effects, another explains RMSE, another distinguishes covariate and concept shift. Correct the misconception that any input drift proves a model failed.

slides.title: Exit: make one prediction for H2
body: Which candidate can represent x1 squared?
State a reason before fitting either model.
payload: Expanded basis: x0, x1, x2, x1^2
Choose on validation, not final test.
slides.teach: One-minute exit. The expanded basis can express the known generator while the linear basis cannot exactly do so. This is representational capability, not a promised test score. H2 begins by freezing the full evaluation protocol.
